strengths: The two proposed losses are well motivated by concrete empirical observations in the paper: unsupervised contrastive loss addresses observed mode collapse for tail classes (Fig. 8-10), while the conditional-unconditional alignment loss is motivated by the observation that conditional and unconditional denoising trajectories share similar low-frequency content at large timesteps (Fig. 3, Fig. 11), drawing a sensible analogy to prior GAN-based long-tail methods (UTLO, Transitional-GAN).

Experimental evaluation is extensive: results are reported on ImageNet-LT (256x256, SiT/DiT), TinyImageNet-LT and Places-LT (UNet/DDPM), and CIFAR10-LT/CIFAR100-LT, across multiple training epochs/steps and both classifier-free guidance sampling budgets (DDIM 10/100 steps, ODE 50 steps, full 1000 steps).

Thorough ablations are provided: individual loss component contribution (Table 4), batch-resampling interaction (Table 5), head/body/tail category breakdown (Table 3), FID for the theoretically optimal balanced-data model as reference, statistical significance across random seeds (Table 10), and qualitative/quantitative mode-collapse diagnostics via t-SNE, density estimation, and nearest-neighbor visualization.
The paper is transparent about limitations, explicitly reporting the ~1.5-1.6x training-time overhead from the extra unconditional forward pass while clarifying that inference latency is unaffected.

Comparisons against relevant and recent baselines (CBDM, OCLT, and the concurrent Dispersive Loss) are included, along with discussion of how the proposed contrastive loss differs conceptually from concurrent/related work (DiffROP, Dispersive Loss, REPA).
weaknesses: The core technical novelty is somewhat incremental: the unsupervised contrastive loss is essentially a batch-uniformity regularizer with no augmented positive pairs (self-similarity as the only 'positive'), which the paper itself acknowledges is very close to the concurrent Dispersive Loss; the distinguishing claim (applied in unconditional latent space and "implicitly" extended to conditional training via the alignment loss) is not strongly isolated or ablated apart from the combined loss table.

The magnitude of improvement shrinks noticeably with more training (e.g., Table 1 Recall improvement over SiT drops from +4.08 at 40 epochs to +2.73 at 160 epochs), raising the question of whether gains persist or vanish with sufficiently long training/larger-scale models.

No experiments on standard (balanced) large-scale ImageNet generation are provided to show the method does not hurt performance in non-long-tailed regimes, despite the framework being proposed as generally applicable to DDPM/SiT training pipelines.

Sensitivity of the method to the key hyperparameters α and γ (loss weighting coefficients) is not analyzed in the main paper or appendix; only the on/off ablation of each loss term is shown, leaving reproducibility of tuning unclear.

Metric reporting is inconsistent across tables (e.g., Precision/Recall reported for ImageNet-LT/SiT but not for CIFAR10-LT/CIFAR100-LT or TinyImageNet-LT/Places-LT tables; FID_tail is reported for UNet-based experiments but not for the flagship ImageNet-LT/SiT results), making cross-dataset comparison of tail-specific gains harder.

The claimed societal benefit ("positive impact on content generation of underrepresented groups") is asserted without deeper discussion of potential failure modes or fairness caveats specific to the proposed alignment mechanism.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and practically relevant problem (long-tailed class-conditional diffusion generation) and clearly grounds the approach in observed phenomena (mode collapse for tail classes; low-frequency similarity between conditional and unconditional denoising at early timesteps, Fig. 3/11).
The two proposed losses (UCL and AL) are simple, architecture-agnostic, and are demonstrated on both UNet-based DDPM/SBDM and Diffusion Transformer (SiT), showing some generality.

Experimental evaluation is broad: five datasets (ImageNet-LT, TinyImageNet-LT, Places-LT, CIFAR10-LT, CIFAR100-LT) at multiple resolutions, several baselines (CBDM, OCLT, Dispersive Loss, UTLO-inspired), ablations on loss components and batch-resampling, super-category (head/body/tail) breakdowns, DDIM-10-step and full 1000-step evaluations, and unconditional generation results.

Good supporting qualitative/diagnostic analysis: t-SNE and kernel-density visualization of synthetic vs. real tail-class images, nearest-neighbor analysis showing reduced memorization/mode collapse, and side-by-side qualitative comparisons across several tail classes.
A short theoretical derivation connects the alignment loss to KL-divergence minimization between conditional and unconditional reverse transitions, giving the method some principled grounding.

The paper is transparent about limitations (extra compute due to two forward passes) and reports statistical-significance checks (albeit only on CIFAR100-LT) and reference numbers for the balanced-data upper bound.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental: the UCL is essentially a negative-only repulsive/contrastive regularizer very close to the concurrent Dispersive Loss (Wang & He, 2025), and the alignment loss is a fairly direct adaptation of the GAN-based UTLO idea (Khorram et al., 2024) to diffusion timesteps; the combination is reasonable but each component individually offers limited new insight.

Claims of improving diversity "without trading off fidelity" are not fully supported by the main results: in Table 1, CCUA's Precision is noticeably lower than Dispersive Loss at 80/120/160 epochs (e.g., 65.80 vs 58.62 at 80 epochs), indicating a real fidelity trade-off that is understated in the text.

No error bars or multiple-seed results are reported for the main large-scale results (Table 1, Table 2, Table 3), which is important given diffusion training stochasticity; statistical-significance analysis is only performed on CIFAR100-LT with DDPM, not for the flagship ImageNet-LT/SiT experiments.

The method incurs non-trivial extra training cost (1.6x DDPM, 1.48x SiT per epoch) due to two forward passes per step, which is a meaningful practical limitation not weighted much in the comparisons (e.g., epoch-matched rather than compute-matched comparisons to baselines).

Evaluation relies solely on standard automatic metrics (FID/sFID/IS/Precision-Recall/KID); no human evaluation or downstream task evaluation (e.g., classifier trained on synthesized data) is provided to corroborate perceptual quality/diversity claims.

Scale of experiments is limited to relatively small resolutions (up to 256×256) and moderate model sizes; it remains unclear whether gains persist at larger-scale, more modern text-to-image or class-conditional generation settings.

The batch-resampling component, while helpful, is adopted from prior work (Zhang et al., 2024) and its interaction with UCL, while ablated, is not deeply analyzed theoretically beyond an intuitive argument.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and practically important problem: mode collapse and low diversity in class-conditional diffusion models trained on long-tailed data.

Proposes a conceptually clean combination of two losses (an unsupervised contrastive/repulsive loss on unconditional latents and a conditional-unconditional alignment loss weighted toward large timesteps) with a reasonable theoretical narrative connecting them via mutual-information decomposition and a KL-divergence derivation that reduces the alignment loss to a simple noise-matching term.

Extensive empirical validation across many datasets (ImageNet-LT at 256x256, TinyImageNet-LT, Places-LT, CIFAR10/100-LT), multiple imbalance factors (0.01 and extreme 0.001), and two backbone families (UNet-based DDPM and DiT/SiT), which is unusually comprehensive for this problem area.

Consistent and often sizeable improvements over relevant baselines (SiT, CBDM, REPA, Dispersive Loss, OCLT, DiffROP) in FID, sFID, IS, precision/recall, and especially FID on tail classes, across different training budgets (250k-900k steps) and sampling schedules (DDIM 10/100 steps).

Thorough ablation studies (loss hyperparameters, batch resampling interaction, choice of latent encoder layer, timestep weighting schedule) that support design choices rather than just reporting a single best configuration.

Good qualitative and analytical support for the core motivating observation (similarity of low-frequency components across classes at early denoising steps, mode collapse visualized via t-SNE/KDE and nearest-neighbor analysis), which strengthens the intuition behind the alignment loss.
Provides a practical efficiency fix (single forward pass for conditional+unconditional) that mitigates the extra training cost, with quantified overhead (~1.3x slower, modest memory increase).
weaknesses: The theoretical justification for the contrastive loss is somewhat informal: treating the anchor as its own positive (no augmentation) is a nonstandard contrastive setup, and the claim that this yields meaningful diversification rather than merely acting as a generic repulsion regularizer is asserted rather than rigorously proven; the mutual-information argument is heuristic rather than a tight bound analysis relevant to generation quality.

Precision sometimes decreases relative to baselines even as FID/recall improve (e.g., Table 5, some configurations), and the fidelity-diversity trade-off is not deeply analyzed or discussed beyond headline metrics.

Experiments are limited to relatively small diffusion backbones (SiT/DiT-B-scale, UNet DDPM); it is unclear whether the gains persist at larger model/data scales or with more modern large-scale conditional generation pipelines, limiting evidence for broader impact.

The interaction between the proposed loss and the batch-resampling strategy is only partially disentangled; while Table 4 shows some decomposition, the main results largely report the combined recipe, making it harder to isolate the contribution of the alignment/contrastive losses alone in the primary tables.

Presentation is dense in places (heavy notation, many appendix tables with inconsistent labeling, e.g., CCUA-N variants), which could hinder reproducibility for readers not carefully cross-referencing appendices; no explicit statement of code release for reproducibility.

Limited discussion of failure modes, societal impact, or scenarios where the alignment loss might hurt controllability (the paper acknowledges this risk briefly but does not empirically probe controllability loss beyond precision/recall).

strengths: Addresses a clearly important and practically relevant problem: mode collapse/lack of diversity for tail classes in class-conditional diffusion models trained on long-tailed data.

The core idea is well motivated both empirically (Fig. 4/7/10/11 show low-frequency similarity between conditional/unconditional denoising at large t, and mode collapse for tail classes) and theoretically (the mutual-information decomposition in Eq. 2 gives a clear, convincing argument for why naively applying contrastive loss directly on conditional latents admits a degenerate shortcut solution, motivating the proposed indirect diversification via unconditional latents + alignment).

Very thorough experimental validation: results are reported across five datasets (ImageNet-LT, TinyImageNet-LT, Places-LT, CIFAR10-LT, CIFAR100-LT), at multiple training checkpoints/imbalance factors, and on both UNet/DDPM and DiT/SiT backbones, showing consistent improvements in FID, FID_tail, IS, sFID, precision/recall, and KID over strong recent baselines (CBDM, REPA, Dispersive Loss, OCLT, DiffROP, UTLO-inspired GAN alignment).

Extensive ablations (loss weight search, batch-resampling interaction, choice of latent encoder depth, alignment-loss time scheduler) support the design choices and show the two losses are complementary/synergistic rather than redundant.

Good qualitative and interpretability analyses beyond FID numbers: t-SNE/density visualizations of tail-class sample distributions, nearest-neighbor analysis exposing literal memorization/mode collapse in the baseline, and frequency decomposition of the reverse process supporting the alignment-loss motivation.

Practical considerations are addressed, including an implementation trick to reduce the ~2x forward-pass overhead to ~1.3x slowdown, and a fair 700k-vs-900k step comparison confirming gains aren't just from extra compute.
Clear attribution/discussion of relationship to concurrent and prior works (Dispersive Loss, CBDM, REPA, UTLO), with explicit discussion of what differs conceptually.
weaknesses: The technical contribution is an incremental but reasonable combination of existing components (InfoNCE-style unsupervised contrastive loss, distillation/alignment loss between conditional and unconditional predictions); novelty lies more in the specific application and combination than in a fundamentally new mechanism.

Diversity claims are argued indirectly via FID/Recall and qualitative visualizations rather than a direct intra-class diversity metric (e.g., pairwise LPIPS within a class), which would more directly substantiate the central diversity claim.

Recall sometimes decreases for CCUA relative to baselines at later training steps (e.g., Table 1 at 900k: CCUA recall 17.3 vs. SiT 18.6, REPA 19.8), which is not discussed despite recall being one of the two headline metrics ("quality and diversity") emphasized in the paper.

The mutual-information argument (Eq. 2) is intuitive but not rigorously formalized (no proof that the trivial/shortcut solution is actually reached in practice for the conditional contrastive baseline, only cited from concurrent work); a more rigorous or empirical direct validation of the claimed shortcut would strengthen the theoretical narrative.

Hyperparameter ablation in Table 5 shows fairly inconsistent trends across (α, γ) combinations (e.g., precision/recall trade-offs move non-monotonically), suggesting some sensitivity to tuning that is not deeply analyzed.

Experiments are capped at 256×256 resolution and up to 900k steps; it remains unclear how benefits scale to larger, longer-trained, or higher-resolution generative pipelines more representative of current large-scale practice.

Minor clarity issues: notation-heavy derivation in Sec. 3.2/3.3 could better foreground intuition before equations, and some inconsistencies in table color-coding descriptions/labels across the appendix reduce readability.
